title: I'm Bad With Names
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article challenges the common excuse 'I'm bad with names,' arguing that forgetting names is really a failure to fix a solvable problem rather than a fixed trait. It claims leaders who don't retain names either don't care enough about the people in front of them or are too focused on their own introduction to listen. The piece offers a concrete technique: repeat the other person's name immediately after hearing it, and again shortly afterward in conversation, to cement it in memory. It frames name recall as a signal of genuine interest that affects a leader's ability to advocate for, connect with, and share information among colleagues. The archivist finds this a practical, technique-driven piece rather than a purely conceptual one.
points: Chronic forgetting of names usually reflects inattention or disinterest, not a fixed cognitive limitation.
Once a name is missed, most people are too embarrassed to ask again, compounding the problem.
The core technique is repeating a new acquaintance's name immediately upon introduction and again soon after.
Using someone's name naturally in conversation ('Casey, thanks for being here') both signals attentiveness and reinforces memory.
Leaders who excuse themselves as 'bad with names' let themselves avoid doing the small, learnable work of getting better.
quotes: Leaders who have trouble remembering the names of those they meet have one of two issues.
They know that once a name is missed, it is exceptionally hard to recover from.
The truth is, unless a person’s short-term memory is significantly impaired, no one is bad at names.
Personal references, including names, invite people into a conversation. Not referring to them by name has the opposite effect.
The touchstone for mastering the skill is simply repeating the other person’s name immediately upon an introduction.
Launching into conversation does not burnish the name into memory, so a good leader must repeat it immediately.
